newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Celltech sees PMA for drug in '98.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Celltech sees PMA for drug in '98.

text.p: UK biotech company Celltech Group Plc said on Monday its leukaemia drug CMA 676 could receive U.S. marketing approval in 1998 if it performed well in a trial scheduled to start next year.

"We hope that a product of this kind might be somewhat safer than conventional chemotherapy, and yet still be able to achieve the killing off of tumour cells," chief executive David Bloxham told Reuters in an interview.
Earlier, the company said a Phase I/II study of 36 nearly-terminal patients suffering from acute myeloid leukaemia in the U.S. showed the drug was remarkably safe.
Bloxham said the company, along with U.S. partner American Home Products Corp, was planning to start another study in early 1997 on less-severe leukaemia cases.
That study will involve 50 "first relapse" patients -- people who have received an initial round of chemotherapy -- and will take place at about 10 U.S. and Canadian centres.

Bloxham said Celltech was aiming for at least 25 to 30 percent of the patients to respond completely to the drug, meaning that their tumour cells would disappear and their white blood counts would return to normal.

"One would hope, with all those data together, that we could then become eventually standard first line therapy. But that will take a number of years to get all the relevant data before that would be the case," Bloxham said.
Celltech's shares shot up 12.5p to 500 by 1130 GMT after it reported the Phase I/II results, which showed the drug's main side effects were fever and chills for short periods.
Bloxham said Celltech, due to report its full-year results on Tuesday, had enough cash on hand to fund its operations.
"We're in a stable financial position," he said.
He declined to forecast the company's results.
"There are no suprises relative to what is expected for Celltech," Bloxham said.
